doc.title: Roswell Rudd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Listening to Cecil Taylor's music
summary: He advises listening for dialogue and tells of a listener who stormed out and then returned nightly to Taylor's music.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: with each other. I mean they were just like firing off guns and stuff, musically, with each other.

If someone who kind of liked jazz was trying to get into that music that you’re describing, most likely would have problems, is that what you would tell them? To try to understand how they’re conversing with each other?

I would say listen for that. Listen for some kind of dialogue. Listen for one guy to say something and see what comes back. See if the components are responding to each other with what they do. And I wouldn’t want to get any more literal than that. And then I’d say if you can’t do that, maybe you can get off on the sound, on the emotion, the totality of the thing, and it certainly had that, it was a huge sound. And the screams that would go right through an ordinary person and probably make them jump up and spin around a few times and then run out. I saw that happen. I saw people reacting that way to Cecil’s music one night when he got into a vortex and somebody got up from their table and started saying, “This is shit, this is shit, I can’t stand it” and went into a vortex themself and ran out into the night. But that same person came back and they couldn’t get rid of them. Came back night after night after night and sat there respectfully and wouldn’t go away, became a regular.
I guess they were getting something they needed.

Exactly. And I think that’s what happens with music on different levels, that people get changed, people get healed, they get revelations, they probably find out more who they are what this while thing is about, through art. Yeah.
